records.title: Scotland Against Spin
records.bodyText:
Our letter in the National today.
A REPORT by the Fraser of Allander Institute at the University of Strathclyde claims that almost 50,000 people are working in the Scottish renewables sector, but it should be taken with a very large pinch of salt. The report was commissioned by Scottish Renewables, so the intent behind it was clearly to propagandise in favour of the Scottish renewable energy industry.
One of the key words running through the report is “estimate”. The jobs turn out to be an estimate of around 49,200 full-time equivalent (FTE) jobs. The estimates, we are told, are also subject to revision as further survey responses are received and as methods are improved. It is based on Office for National Statistics (ONS) survey data with a model of the Scottish economy, because renewable energy is not separately identified in the national accounts. We are also told that survey uncertainty, revisions to official data and an updated economic model mean the results should not be compared directly with previous editions. These caveats, taken together, suggest either that previous reports, or this one, cannot be regarded as truly accurate.
What is the renewable energy sector? Who knows? It is not currently defined by the ONS. Instead, the report has constructed a hypothetical renewable energy sector. It’s difficult to know what that means, but it’s easy to see that the most generous gloss has been put on this – for example, of the 49,200 FTE jobs “supported by” Scotland’s renewable energy sector, 825 are in arts, entertainment and recreation; 350 are in public admin and defence; 375 are in water supply, sewerage and waste; 1135 are in finance and insurance; 200 are in mining and quarrying. And so it goes on, with jobs seemingly being re-labelled to suit the narrative. Almost incredibly, 5050 are said to be in electricity and gas.
The report runs to no more than 12 pages. Its analysis is too short and too simple to allow of detailed scrutiny. For instance, of the jobs said to be supported by the Scottish renewables sector, we are not told how many of the workers concerned are UK citizens and how many are foreign nationals. We know that many of the renewable energy companies working in Scotland and hoovering up taxpayer-funded subsidies are foreign-owned. We know that much of the money paid to them goes abroad. The report fails to analyse such issues.
The front cover image for the report was provided by SSE. I suggest that he who pays the piper calls the tune.
Aileen Jackson
Scotland Against Spin

Scotsman letters
I am surprised a nationalist like Stan Grodynski rails against extracting oil and gas from the North Sea (Letters, 31 October). Doesn’t he remember the SNP slogan “It’s Scotland’s oil”? There are plenty of reserves yet to be extracted from the continental shelf. The companies capable of doing this are taxed at 78 per cent by the UK government. An independent Scotland could attract more investment by reducing that shockingly high rate, and billions would flow into its coffers.
As a geographer, I don’t buy into the argument of the myriad “climate centres” that continuing to extract oil, gas and coal will cause irreversible damage to the planet. We should prepare for climate change rather than try to control the climate of our four billion-year-old Earth, which has had huge variations in climate from one epoch to the next.
How can the “just transition” parrots ignore the environmental damage caused by wind farms scarring Scotland’s once-pristine hills with billions of tons of concrete, and hundreds of miles of bulldozed tracks? How can they ignore the battery yards with thousands of containers full of poisonous substances scarring our lowlands as well as hundreds of miles of new power lines taking electricity from where it’s generated an inordinate distance from markets. I submit that a big 2GW coal-fired power station like Longannet is more environmentally friendly than all the renewables in Scotland.
Talking of coal, geologists have recently discovered a huge one trillion deposit under the Forth which could be extracted using modern techniques such as remote mining. This would allow an independent Scotland to export the “black gold” needed to produce cement and steel, as well as a source of many products.
It’s a strange form of nationalism that won’t use the treasures waiting to be tapped for the benefit of the nation.
William Loneskie Oxton, Lauder, Berwickshire 
John Swinney famously did not want to engage in the questions over the Rosebank oil field at First Minister’s Questions. He only needed to look out of the window of Bute House to get his answer. The number of protestors outside would not fill a bus even if all the tickets were £2 or less. Many Scots are fed up with climate protestors and want Rose bank developed. mrs win ney made a poor judgment if he thought opening Rosebank would have lost him many votes. He has tried to sit on the fence. He has fallen off.
Leaders are meant to lead and be mindful of public sentiment. Mr Swinney is not doing this.
Gerald Edwards
Glasgow

records.bodyText:
You’d be forgiven for thinking that the environmental impact assessment for the Glen Earrach Energy Pumped Storage Hydro scheme is now complete. It is far from it; but don’t just take our word for it….
This is according to Glen Earrach, who have recently part funded a PhD Studentship at Bangor University to the tune of just under £140,000, to evaluate the influence of the GEE Pumped Storage Hydro on the hydro-environmental characteristics of Loch Ness. The research will run until 2029 (https://www.bangor.ac.uk/sos/research-grants-awards).
This research project specifically aims to support the design and implementation of the GEE PSH plant, specifically focusing on Loch Ness (tailpond) and Loch nam Breac Dearga (headpond).
The primary objective is to develop a comprehensive hydro-environmental model for Loch Ness to analyse its thermal and hydrodynamic characteristics and assess how PSH operations may influence stratification and circulation patterns. With a focus on:
• Lake temperature, stratification, and mixing dynamics
• Water movements, including circulation and seiching patterns
Sounds complex but such research into possible impacts should be applauded. This may also help to address some of the concerns raised by the Ness District Salmon Fishery Board - https://ndsfb.org/pump-storage-hydro/
Bangor University have stated ‘by evaluating these potential impacts, the project will provide valuable data and recommendations to guide the planning, construction, and operational phases of the PSH plant’.
This research could make a welcome addition to any environmental impact assessment on PSH, particularly in the unique setting of Loch Ness. But the research findings and recommendations should be presented prior to consenting and building the GEE scheme (if approval is still appropriate). 
Only then will we know that the scheme can progress without disrupting the hydro-environmental dynamics of Loch Ness and its surrounding ecosystem.

records.title: Environmentalists Against Wind Turbines
records.bodyText:
Offshore Wind Farms Shouldn’t Stand Between You and Rescue

By Bonnie Brady
November 02, 2026

https://www.realclearenergy.org/articles/2026/11/02/offshore_wind_farms_shouldnt_stand_between_you_and_rescue_1214451.html

You call the Coast Guard for a medevac out on the water. You are told, “Ten minutes ETA,” provided its helicopter can “make way of the wind farm.”

Huh?


That was the message on Marine Channel 16 on October 14, 2026, when the HOS Rocinante, an offshore wind construction vessel, requested an evacuation in the Sunrise Wind Farm. The helicopter upon arrival at the scene took 12 minutes to descend to the vessel’s helipad. On a clear day. Now imagine you, or a family member, on a boat without a helipad, in darkness, fog or storm.

Whether you are aboard a tugboat, sailboat, ferry, cruise ship or a plane forced into the water, you depend on the same rescuers. But rescuers cannot become the next victims. Your emergency does not pause while they find a safe way to reach you.

Three developments in six weeks demand answers: the discovery of the F/V Mistress, which sank on New Year’s Day 2019; the October 3 Canadian air ambulance crash south of Nantucket; and the October 14 Sunrise Wind farm medevac.

The F/V Mistress was discovered last month 50 feet from Block Island Wind Farm’s (BIWF’s) Turbine 1. Two fishermen, Oscar Diaz and John Ansay Jr., died. They issued a Mayday. Coast Guard records describe a helicopter forced to turn back. But it wasn’t the high winds, poor visibility, and low clouds that forced the helicopter to abort the rescue. The “hazard” was the wind farm.

On October 3, 2026, the William Sparling, a “fast response” Coast Guard cutter, left New London around 1:30 a.m. to search for the HTT104 Canadian air ambulance, which disappeared from radar enroute to Boston. But the cutter was forced to take the long way around the Revolution, Sunrise and Vineyard Wind offshore wind farms, an estimated six extra nautical miles, delaying its arrival by approximately 30 minutes.

The William Sparling search and HOS Rocinante medevac: two rescue operations, eleven days apart. How much rescue time was lost, and why? And what about the Block Island Wind Farm, did it play any role in Mistress’s sinking? How did the wind farm affect the chance of rescue?

The Washington Times reports that Ørsted began maintenance at Turbine One in April 2019, three months after the sinking. A 2020 Bureau of Ocean Energy Management report recorded partial boat debris at the same turbine. Who was notified? What did Ørsted know, and when did they know it?

Ørsted, majority owned by Denmark’s government, had a financial stake in federal approval of South Fork, Revolution Wind and Sunrise Wind offshore wind farms. The Biden administration approved their construction plans in 2022, 2023 and 2024.

Was information about the wreck in 2019 withheld to keep those approvals, and the money, moving? Did protecting those offshore wind farms take precedence over protecting American lives?

Officials were warned: by Raytheon radar pioneer Dr. Eli Brookner in 2008, the Coast Guard in 2020 and the National Academy of Sciences in 2022. Offshore wind farms can obscure boats on radar, increase collision risks and hamper search and rescue.

Green Oceans, the Rhode Island group that identified the wreck and reported finding human remains, called for a federal investigation last month.

The response from those in charge? Crickets. No word of an investigation, not into the Mistress, or the documented delayed responses to Search and Rescue by offshore wind farms.

Then as if to rub salt in the wounds, this Sunday, October 25, the ARIES RAM XII, a jack-up maintenance barge, was seen working beside BIWF’s Turbine One. The Green Oceans report shows spud marks from a similar maintenance vessel on the seabed, feet from the Mistress’s hull.

Why is maintenance being allowed to continue? Shouldn’t someone be trying to retrieve the possible human remains of the fallen crew of the Mistress? The families of the men aboard Mistress deserve answers. So does every family that could face the next emergency out on the water.

President Trump has led the fight against offshore wind. Now we need him to direct a coordinated federal investigation involving the departments of Homeland Security, Interior and Justice to protect the evidence and uncover the truth not only about the Mistress, but about past, present and future compromised search and rescue operations due to offshore wind.


Bonnie Brady is Policy Director at New England Fishermen’s Stewardship Association
REALCLEARENERGY.ORG Offshore Wind Farms Shouldn’t Stand Between You and Rescue

Born on 2 November 1881, Tom Johnston would have celebrated his 145th birthday today.
A journalist, politician and Secretary of State for Scotland during the Second World War, Johnston went on to chair the North of Scotland Hydro-Electric Board (NoSHEB) from 1945 to 1959. This part of the privitised electricity industry later became Scottish & Southerh Energy (SSE). 
His ambition was about far more than generating electricity. Hydro helped bring power, jobs, opportunity and modernisation to communities across the Highlands, changing lives in the process.
A collection of Johnston's original speeches, documents which remarkably survived for years in a box under a colleague's desk, being used as a footrest, saved today in the SSE archive.
So 145 years after his birth, Johnston's remarkable Hydro Electric legacy can still be seen at various locations across the Highlands today.

Nairns Linoleum Factory Kirkcaldy 
The First Factory built In 1847, canvas weaver Michael Nairn built Scotland's first floor-cloth factory in Kirkcaldy, initially nicknamed "Nairn's Folly" due to the financial risk.
After Frederick Walton invented linoleum in the 1860s, Nairn adopted the material and expanded rapidly, eventually making Kirkcaldy the largest producer of linoleum in the world.
The linoleum manufacturing process relying heavily on oxidized linseed oil created a distinct, heavy odor across the town that passing train passengers and locals instantly recognised.
Production eventually shifted from the historic 19th Centery sites, and the iconic Den Road / Victoria Road factory buildings fell into disrepair before being demolished.
Power Station associated with Kirkcaldy works of Michael Nairn & Co (Linoleum manufacturers).
Photo from the 1949 edition of "Turbine Lubrication" published by Wakefield Oil shows the British Thomson Houston (BTH) steam turbines.
Alain Foote supplied the following information regarding BTH turbines. BTH supplied two 3,600kW 3000 r.p.m. turbines type H6Y46 in 1925 (BTH Serial Numbers R1296 & R1297). A further 6,000kW 3000 r.p.m. turbine was supplied in 1935 ( BTH Serial Number R1860).
David Bowie Fife supplied the boiler information.— in Kirkcaldy.

records.bodyText:
Following a public consultation in 2003, North Yell Development Council (NYDC) decided to investigate a community renewable energy project. A study was undertaken which recommended 5 wind turbines with a total capacity of 4.5MW, sited at Garth. Fourteen years later, in 2017, the wind farm was completed at a cost of £8.3 million.
Since this time the windfarm has produced over 90,000 Mwh of energy and has generated funds to enable NYDC to invest in community projects such as the industrial estate extension and marina at the Cullivoe Harbour as well as get Next month is a milestone for North Yell. On 14 July 2026 the  first house purchased by the local development trust will be let, and its new tenant will move in.
It’s an important moment because, like so many areas in rural Scotland, this is a place where there’s nowhere for workers to live – and there’s nowhere for young people to go when they leave home.
So they investing in housing. And the thing that has allowed us to do that is wind. In 2017 we built five wind turbines at Garth wind farm, which together generate around 4.5 MW of electricity that goes right back into the grid.
Every year, they negotiate with suppliers to get the best price for the electricity we produce, and after we have covered costs the rest we invest right back into the community.
The amount of power they generate is the equivalent to just one of the turbines at the Viking Wind Farm on mainland Shetland, which has 103 turbines and is run by Viking and SSE Renewables. But the amount of difference we’ve made in terms of community benefit and investment here is incomparable.
As they had an active and determined volunteer community, they borrowed £8.3m to build it – that was a huge risk for the community to take, but it’s paid off big time.
Each year they need to take in around £1m to cover our costs and anything on top of that we invest back in the community. At the moment we are investing in housing, and before now we have extended our industrial estate, built a big marina, purchased the local shop and bought two business units which are being turned into a community hub.
In addition, running a number of social projects, including a free community lunch club, which is attended by 60-70 people weekly, a local youth club and shopping and prescription deliveries. They have also just purchased a vehicle for community use, and operate a community grant scheme, distributing funds to other organisations and individuals.
It has been confirmed they are the largest community-owned industrial estate in Europe, and it’s occupied by local businesses over 14 sites.
Built a 28-berth marina – with 23 permanently let berths and 5 for visiting vessels. This services business and recreation users, as well as the tourist industry that’s built up in Cullivoe – and
are now planning to build a caravan park.
Unlike some other windfarm developments, there was never any objection to Garth, and that’s because all profits are going back to the community. Now, there are a number of potential projects trying to replicate what we have done but they can’t get a look-in, because there’s no space for them to connect to the local grid. Yell Windfarm can’t expand, either, for the same reason.
This story was told in a report released by Platform on the Social Value of Renewables in the Highlands and Islands. There are other projects, like Tilley, Tiree’s community wind turbine, which returns over 100 times more economic value to the community than the privately-owned Beinn An Tuirc 1-2 Wind Farm, despite being around 1 % of the size.
Community projects should grid connected ahead of large development projects.
As this project has shown what can be done with a fraction of the power that Viking produces – if big developers left a small amount of grid connection aside for others to do what we have done, the benefits would be massive.
Where big windfarms are being developed, the community should receive a percentage of their gross income in the same way as they pay the landowners.
Community benefit should not be calculated based on a £/installed megawatt basis. This is not fair, and current Scottish Government guidance relating to this should be both revised and enshrined in legislation.
Communities should also have a right to buy a share in the renewables project should they wish to do so. And crucially there should be access to the grid for community projects who want to make the most of the clean power that Scotland has to offer.— at North Yell Community Shop Ltd.
